emergency.notes: Both 999 and 112 work for all emergencies. Garda (police) non-emergency: 01-666-9000 (Dublin). Coast Guard: 112 or VHF Channel 16. Mountain Rescue: 112.
emergency.general: Call 999 or 112 for all emergencies — both numbers work throughout the Republic of Ireland for police (Gardaí), ambulance, fire, and coast guard. English is an official language, so communication with emergency services is straightforward. For non-emergency police assistance, contact your local Garda station.

travelAdvisory.summary: Exercise normal precautions in Ireland. Ireland is a stable, safe country and a popular destination for US tourists with close cultural ties.

travelAdvisoryUK.summary: Most visits to Ireland are trouble-free. Be aware of petty crime, particularly in Dublin city center.

healthcare.systemType: Universal (HSE — Health Service Executive) for residents; private for tourists
healthcare.costForTourists: EU visitors with EHIC receive care at Irish public rates. Non-EU tourists pay full cost. GP visit €50-80. Emergency room €100 flat charge at public hospitals. Private hospital stay €500-2,000+/night.
healthcare.pharmacyAccess: Pharmacies (chemists) are widely available in towns and cities. Many OTC medications available. Pharmacists speak English.
healthcare.hospitalNotes: Major public hospitals in Dublin and Cork are well-equipped. Wait times at public emergency departments can be very long (4-12+ hours for non-critical cases). Private hospitals have shorter waits but are expensive.
healthcare.insuranceAdvice: Travel insurance recommended for non-EU visitors. EU citizens should carry EHIC. Private health insurance speeds access to care and avoids long public ER wait times.

pharmacy.hours: Most pharmacies open Mon-Sat 9am-6pm, some late-night pharmacies in cities. Look for 'Pharmacy' or 'Chemist' signs. Some pharmacies open Sunday in city centers.
pharmacy.tips: Pharmacists are well-trained and helpful. Many common OTC medications are available. EU prescriptions are accepted. Some medications available OTC in other countries require prescriptions in Ireland. Emergency contraception is available without prescription from pharmacies.

recommended: meningococcal disease (for students/young adults in close quarters)
vaccinations.notes: No mandatory vaccinations for travelers. Ensure routine vaccinations are current. Ireland has seen mumps outbreaks in recent years — ensure MMR vaccination is up to date.

water.notes: Tap water is safe to drink throughout Ireland. Irish tap water is among the cleanest in the world.

healthcare.foodSafetyTips: Ireland has excellent food safety standards. Traditional foods like fish and chips, Irish stew, and soda bread are safe. Irish dairy and beef are world-class. Be cautious with unfamiliar wild plants. Food in pubs is generally safe.

travelInsurance.requiredNote: Not required but strongly recommended for all travelers.
travelInsurance.tips: Ireland is expensive for healthcare. A hospital emergency room visit can cost 100-200 EUR without insurance. Doctor visits cost 50-80 EUR. Travel insurance with medical evacuation coverage is essential — Ireland's geographic isolation makes medical evacuation costly. EHIC covers EU citizens for emergency care.

healthcare.qualityNotes: High-quality healthcare with well-trained doctors. The public health system (HSE) is good but can have long wait times for non-emergency care. Private healthcare is widely available and more expensive but offers faster access. English is universally spoken. Dublin has several international clinics.

medications.prescriptionRules: EU prescriptions are accepted. Prescriptions from outside Ireland may need verification by an Irish doctor. Ireland follows EU pharmaceutical regulations. Some medications have different legal status than in other countries.

restrictedMeds.name: Codeine-containing medications
restrictedMeds.note: Codeine products (like Nurofen Plus) require a prescription in Ireland above small quantities. Some codeine preparations are available OTC in small doses, but higher-strength products require prescription.

restrictedMeds.name: Tramadol
restrictedMeds.note: Controlled opioid. Requires prescription. Carry your foreign prescription and doctor's letter.

restrictedMeds.name: Benzodiazepines (Valium, Xanax, etc.)
restrictedMeds.note: Controlled. EU regulations apply. Carry doctor's letter and original prescription. Customs inspections occur for controlled substances.

restrictedMeds.name: ADHD medications (Adderall, Ritalin, Vyvanse)
restrictedMeds.note: Strictly controlled. Requires Irish prescription or special license. Contact the Irish Health Products Regulatory Authority (HPRA) before traveling with ADHD medications. Carry full documentation.

restrictedMeds.name: Medical cannabis
restrictedMeds.note: Medical cannabis is legal in Ireland under specific circumstances via the Medical Cannabis Access Programme, but it's highly restricted. Recreational cannabis is illegal. CBD products with <0.2% THC are legal.

medications.bringDocumentation: Carry a doctor's letter in English listing all medications with generic names. Keep medications in original packaging. EU citizens should carry EHIC. Non-EU travelers should carry original prescriptions and multilingual medical certificates. For controlled substances, carry a Schengen-style certificate if available.
medications.generalAdvice: Ireland allows travelers to bring a reasonable personal supply of prescription medications (typically up to 3 months) in original packaging with a valid prescription or doctor's letter. For controlled drugs under the Misuse of Drugs Acts, carry your prescription and a doctor's letter explaining the medical necessity. Cannabis and cannabis-derived products (including most CBD oils with any THC) are controlled substances in Ireland. Keep all medications in their original labeled containers for customs inspection.

controlledSubstances.note: Prescription required. Carry original packaging and doctor's letter. Controlled under Misuse of Drugs Act.
Controlled substance. Allowed with valid prescription. Carry doctor's letter, original packaging, and max 3-month supply for personal use.
Cannabis is illegal for recreational use. Medical cannabis access programme exists for residents. CBD products with <0.2% THC are legal.

Available in pharmacies without prescription. Personal supply in original packaging is fine.
Illegal under the Misuse of Drugs Act. Note: fresh magic mushrooms were briefly legal due to a loophole (closed 2006).

scams.description: A stranger approaches and asks you to take their photo with what looks like an expensive camera. You take the shot and hand it back, but they fumble and drop it — or claim you dropped it — and it 'breaks.' They become agitated and demand you pay for the camera, which they claim cost hundreds of e...

scams.name: Fake Charity Collectors
scams.description: You're approached by someone with a vest and a collection tin claiming to raise funds for a well-known charity. The name sounds familiar and the logo looks right, but the person has no official ID or collection permit. The money goes straight to their pocket — not to any charity whatsoever.

scams.name: Friendly Bar Overcharging
scams.description: You're exploring Temple Bar when two cheerful locals strike up a conversation and invite you to 'the best local pub around the corner.' The drinks keep coming and everyone seems friendly. When the bill arrives, you're charged three times the normal rate — the bar is in on it and the 'locals' get ...

scams.name: Phone Snatching
scams.description: You're standing on Grafton Street taking a photo or scrolling your phone when someone on a bicycle or on foot grabs it from your hands and sprints or rides away. It happens in seconds with no warning. Luas stops and busy shopping streets are particularly common spots, especially in the evening ho...

scams.name: Overpriced tourist accommodation
scams.description: Dublin has notoriously high accommodation costs. Some guesthouses and hostels in tourist areas charge premium prices for poor-quality rooms.
scams.avoidance: Book well in advance on established platforms. Read recent reviews carefully. Consider staying outside the city center for better value.

scams.name: Taxi overcharging at night
scams.description: Some taxis overcharge late at night, particularly after pub closing time when demand is high. 'Surge pricing' equivalents are claimed.
scams.avoidance: Use Free Now (formerly MyTaxi) or Uber apps for transparent pricing. Confirm the fare before getting in any taxi.

scams.name: Temple Bar tourist trap pricing
scams.description: Pubs and restaurants in the Temple Bar area charge significantly more than equivalent establishments a few streets away.
scams.avoidance: Temple Bar is worth seeing, but for a proper pint at local prices, walk a few streets north or south of the river.

connectivity.simOptions: SIM cards from Three, Eir, or Vodafone at airports and phone shops. Tourist SIM ~€10-20 for 10-30GB. EU SIM holders can use EU roaming rules. eSIM via Airalo or Holafly.
connectivity.wifiAvailability: Free WiFi widely available in pubs, cafes, restaurants, hotels, and many public areas. Dublin has extensive free public WiFi. Rural areas have improved connectivity.
connectivity.bestOption: Three Ireland SIM for best coverage nationwide including rural areas. EU travelers can use home SIMs under EU roaming.

cultural.tipping: 10-15% is standard in restaurants for good service. Not expected in pubs when ordering at the bar. Taxis: round up or add a euro. Hotel porters: €1-2 per bag.
cultural.dressCode: Casual and practical — the weather changes quickly so layers are essential. Smart casual for restaurants. Pubs are informal. Churches require modest dress.
cultural.greetings: Friendly and informal. 'Howaya' or 'How are you' is a greeting, not a literal question. Irish people are generally warm, chatty, and welcoming to visitors.
taboos: Commenting negatively about Irish culture, sport, or history to locals
Referring to the Republic as 'Southern Ireland' — it is simply 'Ireland'
Being unfriendly or aloof — Irish social culture expects warmth

phrases.local: Thank you / Go raibh maith agat (Irish)
phrases.phonetic: thank yoo / guh rev mah a-gut

safety.lgbtSafety: Excellent. Ireland legalized same-sex marriage in 2015 through a popular referendum — the first country to do so by popular vote. Dublin has a vibrant LGBTQ+ scene. Very welcoming nationwide.
safety.soloFemaleSafety: Very safe. Ireland ranks highly for gender equality. Normal urban precautions apply at night in Dublin city center.
safety.notes: Ireland is one of the safest countries for tourists. Main concerns are petty theft in busy Dublin areas, road safety (narrow rural roads, driving on the left), and rapidly changing Atlantic weather. The Cliffs of Moher and coastal areas can be dangerous — stay behind safety barriers.

practical.visaFreeCountries: US citizens: 90 days visa-free. UK citizens: Common Travel Area (unlimited access). EU citizens: freedom of movement.
practical.bestTimeToVisit: May-September for warmest, driest weather. June-August is peak season. Shoulder seasons (April-May, September-October) offer fewer crowds. Weather is unpredictable year-round — always pack a waterproof layer.

immediate: Stay indoors and away from windows during named storms (Status Red or Orange warnings)
Secure loose outdoor furniture and objects before the storm arrives
Avoid coastal areas, piers, and exposed cliffs during storm surges
Do not drive through flooded roads — even shallow water can be dangerous
Keep phone charged and monitor Met Éireann warnings
after: Check your property for structural damage before re-entering
Report power outages to ESB Networks: 1800 372 999
Avoid downed power lines — assume all lines are live
Check Civil Defence for local assistance
resources: Office of Public Works flood info: www.floods.ie
